To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

FeLV infection of a cat can be divided into two phases, an initial viremia phase and a later disease phase, that the viremia phase can persist for years, and that cats with persistent viremia excrete infectious virus in their saliva.
cats that develop FeLV-induced disease have a prolonged viremia that is associated with the development of FeLV in saliva.
cats that become infected with FeLV may remain healthy for many years before they develop FeLV-induced neoplasias or non-neoplastic disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the epidemiology and pathogenesis of feline leukemia virus infections.
the development of a feline leukemia virus vaccine, the immunologic response to the vaccine, and the development of diagnostic tests for FeLV infections.
the pathogenesis, epidemiology, and immunology of feline leukemia virus infections in domestic cats.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the FeLV-infected cat population is a dynamic system in which infected cats are constantly being added and lost from the pool of infected cats and in which infected cats that are not lost from the system can be expected to remain in the system for long periods of time.
the presence of FeLV in saliva and the persistence of viremia are associated with the development of leukemia or lymphoma.
FeLV infections are not always benign and that the disease may not be apparent for years after infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the FeLV-infected cat population is composed of 2 distinct groups: those with chronic viremia and those with acute viremia.
cats with FeLV-induced disease have a high virus load, while cats without disease have a low viral load, and the virus load in cats that develop non-neoplastic disease is intermediate.
FeLV infection is an important and common cause of disease in cats, and that the disease process is initiated by the virus infection, not the host immune response to the virus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cats can maintain chronic viremia for long periods of time and excrete infectious FeLV in saliva.
cats can be viremic for years without showing any clinical symptoms.
FeLV-infected cats are capable of excreting virus for prolonged periods of time and can be considered infectious for the entire period of viremia.
